old_caption: The video showcases a close-up view of a single, large, cushion-cut diamond with a vibrant yellow hue. The diamond is positioned on a reflective surface, which creates a mirror-like reflection beneath it. The camera remains stationary throughout the sequence, focusing intently on the diamond's facets and the way light interacts with its surfaces. As the video progresses, the highlights and reflections on the surface below shift and change, mirroring the changing light conditions and enhancing the visual appeal. The background is a plain, neutral gray, ensuring that all attention remains on the diamond itself. There are no other objects or characters present in the scene, allowing for an uninterrupted focus on the gemstone's beauty and craftsmanship.

caption: The video showcases a single yellow, cushion-cut faceted gemstone positioned above a smooth reflective surface against a plain light-gray background, with a mirror image visible directly below it. Throughout the video the stone turns slowly in place, its silhouette tilting as the girdle corners shift. A small dark facet near the right-center in the early frames remains visible near the right edge, shifting only slightly as the stone turns. Meanwhile a bright white highlight grows and moves across the upper-center table facet, becoming most prominent later in the video. The reflection beneath tracks these same facet and highlight changes, confirming it mirrors the rotating stone. The gemstone stays roughly centered with only minor drift, and the gap between it and its reflection remains approximately constant. The background and surface show no independent motion.

endpoints are normal, not physical errors. Do not add unseen causes, onset, stopping or outcomes.
An internal editing cut is not evidence of physical motion connecting the views.

Check identification before physical interpretation: a reflection is not a separate actor;
a powder/smoke/liquid outline or shadow is not automatically the boundary of a solid object;
an apparent change caused by occlusion/viewpoint is not automatically material deformation.
Do not claim contact, bending, compression, melting, disintegration or structural recovery unless
the appropriate material/surface itself provides visible evidence. Do not infer a force or earlier

camera tracking. A single visible texture/seam does not prove spin. Avoid unnecessary absolute
claims of stillness, no motion, no camera motion or 'exactly' synchronized changes.
Remove invented scene details and explanations, but keep clearly visible ongoing motion and
processes. Avoid deleting the real process merely because its cause lies outside the cropped window.
